claim: Keeping the best result so far, when quality can be recognised by a real check, makes an anytime procedure monotone in time; without a check, best-so-far is undefined.
agent_test: Compare submit-latest vs submit-best-by-check at equal tokens on held-out items.
audit_note: Zilberstein (1996) states exactly this (monotonicity guaranteed by returning best result so far when quality is recognizable); the two Zilberstein entries are the same paper and the other listed papers do not address the guarantee, so it rests on one source, though the claim is close to definitional.

claim: A contract algorithm (fixed budget, may return nothing if cut) can be turned into an interruptible one by repeated runs with doubling budgets, with worst-case time penalty factor 4 (q_B(4t) >= q_A(t)).
agent_test: Run attempts at b, 2b, 4b banking the best passing answer vs one run at full budget; score at random interrupt points.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-01 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Allocating time among several anytime modules is NP-complete in the strong sense; optimal splits exist only for tree-structured, input-monotone cases, so stage budgets in a multi-stage scaffold must be heuristic. Gap search: one empirical stage-split study exists (Plan and Budget, d08) and one stage-spend result (R2E-Gym, d06); no greedy or learned-profile comparison.
agent_test: Compare fixed shares, greedy marginal gain and learned profiles for stage budgets at equal total tokens.

claim: Zilberstein's Theorem 5 shows myopic value-of-computation stopping is optimal when the performance profile is increasing and concave-down and the cost of time is increasing and concave-up; LLM quality-vs-thinking curves are often non-concave (rise then fall), so a single marginal-gain stop rule is not guaranteed safe.
agent_test: Plot quality vs tokens on our items; count items with plateau-then-jump; test the stop rule against a hard cap plus a check.
audit_note: Zilberstein's Theorem 5 states myopic value-of-computation monitoring is optimal when the profile is increasing and concave-down and time cost is increasing and concave-up (a sufficient condition), not 'only' then; the LLM non-concavity evidence is a synthesis, not a measured concavity test.
claim_before_audit: Myopic value-of-computation stopping is optimal only for concave increasing profiles with convex time cost; LLM quality-vs-thinking curves are often non-concave, so a single marginal-gain stop rule is unsafe.

claim: LLM quality is not monotone in thinking length: it can rise then fall (82.2 to 87.3 then 70.3 percent in one Ghosal panel) and on built tasks it falls (Opus 4 from near 100 to 80-90 percent; R1 70 to 30 percent with five distractors).
agent_test: Measure accuracy at 4 thinking budgets per item; flag longer-is-worse items; test best-by-check vs latest.
audit_note: Minor: Gema reports Opus 4 falling to about 85-90% (an evidence line also says about 80%); all figures match.

claim: Inverse-scaling tasks were built adversarially, so they bound the failure rather than give its prevalence; Opus 4 figures differ by task (85-90 percent Misleading Math, about 80 percent Misleading Python).
agent_test: Estimate the share of our real items that show longer-is-worse behaviour.

claim: Reasoning models overthink easy items: the first solution round is correct in over 92 percent of cases and uses under 60 percent of tokens; 1,953 percent more tokens than conventional models for 2+3.
agent_test: Stop at the first verified answer on easy items; compare tokens and accuracy with the full run.

claim: Early exit and early stopping save compute at little or no accuracy cost: training-free DEER cuts chains by an average 19.1-80.1% with +0.3 to +5.0% accuracy; training-free ESC cuts 34-84% of samples with comparable accuracy; a trained hidden-state probe used as an exit rule cuts 24% of tokens with no performance loss.
agent_test: Exit on agreement of independent trial answers or a code check; compare with model self-confidence at equal tokens.
audit_note: Numbers match (DEER 19.1-80.1% shorter chains with +0.3 to +5.0% accuracy, ESC -34% to -84% samples, probe -24% tokens), but the hidden-state probe is a trained probe, so it is not training-free, and ESC saves samples rather than chain tokens.
claim_before_audit: Training-free early exit saves tokens at little or no accuracy cost: DEER 19.1-80.1 percent shorter chains with +0.3 to +5.0 percent accuracy; ESC cuts 34-84 percent of samples; hidden-state probe cuts 24 percent of tokens.

claim: Self-reported confidence as an exit signal needs per-model thresholds and hurts on code where trial answers are long; external checks are safer.
agent_test: Compare stop-on-self-confidence vs stop-on-verifier at equal tokens.

claim: The best use of a test-time budget depends on item difficulty: beam search or sequential for hard or low budget, best-of-N for easy or high budget; compute-optimal allocation matches best-of-N with up to 4x less compute (PaLM 2, MATH). All lines come from one paper.
agent_test: Cheap difficulty probe then route budget; compare with uniform budget at equal tokens.

claim: Repeated-sampling coverage grows log-linearly over four orders of magnitude (SWE-bench Lite 15.9 to 56 percent at 250 samples) but verifier-free selection plateaus near 100 samples. All lines come from one paper.
agent_test: On items with a real check, measure coverage vs voting accuracy as k grows.

claim: Parallel independent attempts with voting can beat extending one trace at equal budget (up to 20-22 percent at 16K tokens, Ghosal; shortest-first parallel halting saves up to 40 percent tokens, Hassid), but s1 found sequential extension extrapolates better than voting in its setup. Gap search: the split tracks whether the model was trained to use continuation and whether the critic is informative (Zeng: Wait extension on untuned QwQ/R1/LIMO turns right answers wrong more than the reverse; Balachandran: sequential wins on TSP-easy, parallel on AIME). Still contested for trained models.
agent_test: Split a fixed budget into 1, 2, 4 independent attempts vs one long trace; score by check on the same items.

claim: Budget forcing gives an interruptible LLM: s1-32B AIME24 50.0 to 56.7 with Wait; the gain is small against a 30-question test (one item = 3.3 points); extension flattens and 12 of 30 questions overflow context at 512 steps. One paper. Gap search: no replication found; multi-seed work shows 5-15 point seed SD on 30-item sets (d11), so a 6.7-point single-run gain is not distinguishable from noise.
agent_test: Use at least 100 items per cell; replicate forced stop on another model.

claim: In s1's fine-tuned model, a prompt-stated token limit controlled length only 40% of the time (token-conditional control, Table 3) while hard truncation via budget forcing gave 100% control; but hard truncation loses accuracy at small budgets (L1, a length-trained model, is 20-25 points absolute better than s1 at 512-1024 tokens).
agent_test: Use hard caps plus a banked answer rather than a prompted limit.
audit_note: s1 shows token-conditional prompting gave only 40% control for its own fine-tuned model (hard truncation/budget forcing gave 100%), so '40 percent' is the failure of prompting, not of truncation, and 'current models' overgeneralises one model; L1's 20-25 point absolute gain over s1 at 512-1024 tokens is correct, and TALE reports prompt budgets do shrink CoT.
claim_before_audit: Prompt-stated token limits do not control length in current models; hard truncation does (token-conditional control 40 percent in s1 Table 3) but hard truncation loses accuracy at small budgets (L1: 20-25 points absolute better at 512-1024 tokens).

claim: Training can make reasoning anytime-safe: AnytimeReasoner beats GRPO at every budget on a 1.5B model (AIME24 22.9 vs 19.0; 5-benchmark mean at 8000 tokens 46.0 vs 43.0) and E1 protects the solution segment (AIME24 35.0 vs 27.1 L1-Max). Gap search: no multi-seed replication found; same noise caveat as K13.
agent_test: Not testable without training; the scaffold analogue is reserving a final-answer segment. Both are small-model math with no seed variance.

claim: Reserving budget for the final answer (separating thinking and solution budgets) is a cheap anytime safeguard. Gap search: on untrained open models, cutting a trace and forcing an answer works but leaks reasoning into the answer (answers up to 10x longer, d09), so reserve and count the answer segment.
agent_test: Reserve 15-20 percent of tokens for answering from the partial trace; compare with no reservation under random cuts.
audit_note: Minor: E1 separates thinking and solution budgets and Wu et al. report up to 10x longer answers after hard interrupts; 'cheap' is the researcher's judgment (E1's robustness comes with a light GRPO training stage) and the leakage was shown on Qwen3, GPT-OSS and Magistral.

claim: Skipping thinking and sampling many short answers beats thinking at low budgets (ACM 23 at 700 tokens: 51.3 vs 28.9).
agent_test: At low budgets compare one thinking run vs N no-think samples with a check.

claim: Optimal chain length follows an inverted U, rising with difficulty and falling with model capability (14 steps at 1.5B to 4 at 72B).
agent_test: Estimate optimal length per difficulty bin on our model.
audit_note: Wu et al. (2502.07266) states the inverted U and 14 steps at 1.5B to 4 at 72B (Qwen2.5 series), but the second line is the same paper and Su et al. only corroborates overthinking easy problems, so the specific claim rests on one study.

claim: The Illusion-of-Thinking collapse at high complexity is contested: output limits and impossible instances may explain it.
agent_test: Rerun with compact answer forms and solvability checks; do not rely on the collapse claim.

claim: Offline (sleep-time) thinking cuts test-time compute about 5x at equal accuracy when queries share context.
agent_test: Precompute notes on stable context before the query; compare tokens at equal accuracy.

claim: The early rise in the rise-then-fall curve may be added output variance rather than better reasoning (Ghosal model), a competing explanation.
agent_test: Measure answer variance by budget; check whether the early gain vanishes under majority vote.

claim: Metalevel computation selection is a Bayesian selection problem, not a bandit; bandit policies lack a stopping rule.
agent_test: Compare a myopic value-of-information rule with a fixed-count rule.

claim: Stopping when independent trial answers agree saves 15-84 percent of samples or tokens at no or tiny accuracy cost: Adaptive-Consistency 2.4-3.8x fewer samples, ESC -34% to -84%, DeepConf consensus stop -52.8% tokens at K=512 with identical accuracy. Outside math the evidence is thin: MBPP 23.21 fewer samples out of 30 (about -77%, ESC), code +0.4% accuracy at 2.4x (Adaptive-Consistency), GPQA-D only multiple choice.
agent_test: Replace a fixed count of trial attempts by agreement stop (window of 5, tau 0.95); compare accuracy and tokens on held-out code and multi-step items.
audit_note: ESC on MBPP (max 30 samples) used 6.79 samples, a reduction of 23.21 samples (about 77%), not -23%; other figures (AC 2.4-3.8x, ESC -34% to -84%, DeepConf consensus stop -52.8% at K=512 with no accuracy change) match.
claim_before_audit: Stopping when independent trial answers agree saves 15-84 percent of samples or tokens at no or tiny accuracy cost: Adaptive-Consistency 2.4-3.8x fewer samples, ESC -34% to -84%, DeepConf consensus stop -52.8% tokens at K=512 with identical accuracy. Outside math the evidence is thin: MBPP -23% samples (ESC), code +0.4% accuracy at 2.4x (Adaptive-Consistency), GPQA-D only multiple choice.

claim: No head-to-head at equal tokens exists between agreement or real-check stopping and model self-confidence stopping (DEER). Agreement and trained probes each beat fixed-count stops (probe: 87.4 vs about 82.5 percent at similar tokens on MATH), but each was only compared against fixed-count or majority-vote baselines.
agent_test: Three-arm test at equal tokens: DEER-style self-confidence stop, agreement stop, real-check stop, on math and on code.

claim: On code and software tasks the reliable anytime signal is a real execution check; model-written tests alone gave no gain over public tests (S*), and each single verifier plateaued at 42-44 percent on SWE-bench Verified until execution-based and execution-free signals were combined (51.0 percent).
agent_test: On code items compare stop-by-public-tests vs stop-by-model-written-tests vs hybrid, at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: S* attributes the no-gain result to generated tests in selection/debugging ablations (Table 3, Section 5); R2E-Gym plateaus 43.7% and 42.8% then hybrid 51.0% match.

claim: Selection quality and coverage on agent tasks show plateaus and late jumps: QwQ-32B-Preview coverage plateaus beyond N=32 (S*), verifier-selected SWE-bench plateaus near 43 percent then rises to 51 percent with a hybrid, and later reasoning episodes can lower accuracy (MRT, 41-45 episodes). No study fitted a concavity test directly; the best available metric is cumulative regret over the budget curve (MRT).
agent_test: Log quality at 5 budget points per item class; report area under the curve and the share of items whose curve is non-concave.
audit_note: Minor: S* QwQ plateau beyond N=32 and MRT 41-45 episodes (later episodes do not improve, maj@p better) and R2E-Gym 43.7/42.8 to 51.0 match; the 'no study fitted a concavity test' part is an absence claim that cannot be verified.

claim: Per-stage budgets beat a single global token cap (E3 +14% MATH-500, +24% NaturalInstructions, +33% TravelPlanner); the shape of the per-stage schedule matters little (uniform vs decay within a few percent; front-loaded best on planning). Moving rollouts from the solver stage to the test-writing stage gave about twice the marginal gain on SWE-bench (+1.7 vs +0.8 points). Single studies, authors' own metric and no intervals.
agent_test: Compare global cap, equal shares and front-loaded shares across S1-S9 at the same total tokens; also try shifting 20 percent from generation to checking.

claim: Extending one trace with Wait or Alternatively on untrained reasoning models gives weak, model-dependent sequential gains: revision flipped correct answers to wrong more often than the reverse for QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5B (successful revisions were under 10% everywhere), while R1-Distill-32B/14B and LIMO had higher successful than failed revision rates that plateaued after about 10 steps; correct solutions are shorter than wrong ones. The s1 result (sequential extension helps) holds for a model fine-tuned on 1k traces, so the Ghosal vs s1 conflict may be partly explained by training for continuation and critic quality.
agent_test: On our model, measure correct-to-wrong vs wrong-to-correct flips under forced continuation before allowing any extension step.
audit_note: Zeng et al. find failed revisions exceed successful ones only for QwQ and R1-Distill-1.5B; for R1-Distill-32B/14B and LIMO successful revision was higher (though plateauing after about 10 steps), so 'net harmful for QwQ, R1-Distill and LIMO' is too broad.
claim_before_audit: Extending one trace with Wait or Alternatively on untrained reasoning models is net harmful: revision flipped correct answers to wrong more often than the reverse for QwQ, R1-Distill and LIMO, and correct solutions are shorter than wrong ones. The s1 result (sequential extension helps) holds for a model fine-tuned on 1k traces, so the Ghosal vs s1 conflict is explained, not settled, by training for continuation and by critic quality.

claim: Seed variance on 30-item benchmarks is 5-15 points SD, one AIME24 item is 3.3 points, and about 30 seeds are needed for stable means; most RL gains over R1-Distill vanished under paired tests. Single-run gains of 3-7 points on AIME24 (s1, AnytimeReasoner) cannot be trusted without multi-seed confirmation. No direct replication of either paper was found.
agent_test: Use at least 10 seeds and paired tests, and test sets of 100+ items, before accepting any budget-policy gain.

claim: A cheap difficulty probe from answer stability (Certaindex) correlates with steps-to-solution (mean r=0.52) and saves 9-52 percent tokens, but another group found the Certaindex early-exit baseline lost 8 points on MATH-500 (81.44 vs 89.76 percent). Learned budget predictors (SelfBudgeter, 61 percent length cut) need RL training and are math-only. Snell's up to 4x saving was not reproduced outside MATH and PaLM 2.
agent_test: Run a 3-sample stability probe per item, bin by agreement, and check whether per-bin optimal budgets differ by 2x or more.

claim: No LLM study of a doubling-budget schedule (contract to interruptible, factor 4) and no LLM use of Hansen-Zilberstein non-myopic monitoring was found. The nearest result is that per-step curve-fitting beats a static threshold by only 1-3.4 percent of tokens (Certaindex appendix), and that cumulative regret over the budget curve is a usable training objective (MRT).
agent_test: Simulate doubling budgets b,2b,4b with banked best-by-check answer vs known-budget single run on 100+ items; report extra tokens.

claim: Human evidence for the anytime shape is limited to saturating speed-accuracy curves in simple choices and a modest expert penalty under time cuts: 23 grandmasters made 5.02 blunders per 1,000 moves in classical chess and 6.85 in rapid chess (+36.5 percent). Satisficing with aspiration adjustment was not tested against an anytime stopping rule in any source opened.
agent_test: Not directly testable on the agent; use as prior that early quality is high for pattern-matched items.
